DETERMINATION OF THE ACID NUBER OF TRANSFOR' ER AND SWITCHGEAR
INSULATING OILS
PURPOSE
Transformer oil in service for more than 12 years should be checked
by the Chief Chemist for the acid number.
Oil showing an acid number
above .60 has deteriorated to such an extent that it should be discarded.
(Safety Bulletin #6, page 4)
DEFINITION AND SUMMARY
Acid number of an oil is the number of milligrams of KOH to react
with one gram of oil. This number is determined by heating the sample
in contact with an alcohol-water solution and the resulting two phase
mixture titrated hot with aqueous KOH solution using phenolphthalein as
an indicator.
REAGENTS
(1) .1 normal KOH solution (carbonate free).
(2) .1 normal H2S04 solution.
(3) Alcohol solution:
Dilute formula 30 denatured alcohol with an equal volume of
distilled water.
(The method specifies a mixture of methanol and
ethanol corresponding to the composition of formula 30 alcohol.)
(4) Indicator:
1 gram phenolphthalein in 100 ml alcohol.
PROCEDURE
(a) Mix 10 grams of oil sample with 100 ml of alcohol solutione Heat
in 3-5 minutes to boiling, swirling while heating to prevent bump-
ing.
(b) Add 1 ml of phenolphthalein solution.
(c) Titrate to a point where color shows more than momentarily while
swirling. This is the approximate end point.
(d) Add 50 ml of distilled water while swirling and shake mixture,
(e) Observe first 3-5 ml of separated alcohol solution.
If color per-
sists skip paragraph (f).
(f) If no color exists continue to add .l normal KOH in .2 ml amounts
until color persists in first 3-5 ml of alcohol solution.

(e) Sugar-Soluble Ca0:
Weigh out 10 grams, reduce to a milk with water,
and rinse into a 100 ml flask.
Add 20 grams of granulated sugar and dissolve by
the addition of water, or add the same amount of sugar in the form of a freshly pre-
pared sugar solution, e. g. 50 ml of a solution containing 400 grams of sugar per
liter, or 25 ml of a solution made by dissolving 500 grams of sugar in 300 grams of
water (a solution of approximately 62° Brix).
Fill to the mark with water, stopper
the flask, shake gently for two or three minutes until most of the saccharate goes
into solution, then allow to stand 30 minutes, shaking every 5 to 10 minutes during
the period of standing.
Filter, rejecting the first runnings, and titrate 50 ml
of the filtrate with standard Steffen nitric acid (1 ml= .05 gram Cao), using phenol-
phthalein as indicator.
The number of milliliters of acid required represents the

Preparation of sample
After mixing individually the samples of cold and hot saccharate cake described
in sections 8 and 9, prepare by weight a composite of suitable amount in the same pro-
portion by weight as the relative amounts of cold and hot saccharate produced according
to the laboratory records.
Analysis
(a) Apparent purity: The following special apparatus is needed: a carbonator
with steam and carbon dioxide gas connections and an evaporator heated by steam, both so
constructed as to obviate any possibility of burning the juice.
Suitable apparatus is
described in the Chemical Bulletin, po 419, and in drawings SS-195-19, SS-196-19, and
SS-197-19.
Mix a suitable amount of the cake with water of low solids content until a homo-
geneous mixture is obtained; the amount of water used should be such that the filtrate
after subsequent carbonation will have a density of 5 to 6 degrees Brix.
Transfer to
the laboratory carbonator, heat to 80-85°, and carbonate at this temperature to faint
alkalinity with phenolphthalein.
Do not carbonate to neutrality or acidity.
When the
carbonation is finished, heat to boiling, and filter.
Concentrate sufficient of the
filtrate to 20-23° Brix in the laboratory evaporator, being careful not to carry the
evaporation beyond this point on account of the danger of burning the juice.
Draw off
the liquid into a copper can and carbonate again in a laboratory hot water bath to faint
alkalinity.
Filter under vacuum through a Buchner funnel.
Cool the filtrate in a
cylinder and determine the apparent purity as described in the General Methods, Chapter 1,
Section 4.

The move is seen as a rebuke to FTC Chairman Michael Pertschuk, who
has made clear his opposition to some forms of children's advertising.
Consumer groups see it as a defeat. Bob Choate, head of the Council
on Children, Media and Merchandising, said his group "deplores the
action taken by the appropriations committee which voted to restrict
the FTC's inquiries and give major food and advertising companies
another year to use fantasy and frivolity in place of nutritional
facts when selling to children."
OSHA INSPECTION RULING
The Supreme Court decision barring
MINI-VICTORY AT BEST
Occupational Safety and Health
Administration inspectors from
making warrantless searches
probably is not the business victory that some have hailed it.
In a key paragraph, the court ruled that probable cause "in the criminal
law sense" is not required to get a warrant. OSHA could just cite an
industry's high accident rate as cause for an inspection.
The might mean inspection delays, in some cases, but OSHA Administrator
Eula Bingham hopes most companies will let inspectors in without a
warrant.
"This is not going to provide new ways for employers to
escape their responsibility to provide a safe working place," she
said.
MECHANICALLY DEBONED MEAT
Over the objections of consumer groups,
SEEN GAINING USDA APPROVAL
the Agriculture Department will permit
the sale of mechanically deboned meat.
The meat industry contends that federal approval will make an additional
one billion pounds of beef available to consumers, a compelling argument
in the face of shrinking cattle herds. Consumer groups such as the
Community Nutrition Institute, however, have wanted a moratorium until
research answers more health and safety questions.
Government scientists have found mechanically processed beef to be safe,
according to USDA Assistant Secretary Carol Foreman. Packages will
have to state that the meat contains up to .06 percent powdered bone."
AGENCY RECOMMENDS REDUCTION
Chemicals in drinking water "present
OF CHEMICALS IN WATER SUPPLY
a potential risk of cancer that
should be reduced to the extent
feasible, I Dr. Arthur Upton,
director of the National Cancer Institute, said in a recent letter to
the Environmental Protection Agency.
'Exposure to even very small amounts of cancer-causing chemicals poses
some risk and repeated exposure amplifies the risk," Upton said.
EPA has proposed the first phase of a program to reduce cancer-causing
chemicals in drinking water. A hearing on the proposed standards will
take place July 11 and 12 in Washington.

Esso Resources Canada Limited, together with Mobil Oil Canada Ltd., Norcen
Energy Resources Limited and Voyager Petroleums Ltd., announced today that

Technology Name & Description:
Expanded Shredded Stems (ESS)
RJR developed a superheated, pressurized steam process to expand stems. The expanded stems come
out dry and varying in size. The expanded stems must be re-conditioned, screened, and the oversize
material cut to produce usable filler material. Most stem materials can be processed into high filling value
filler material using this process. RJR Filling capacity values from 450 to over 1000 CFC can be attained
depending on stem type and throughput rate. RJR utilized primarily an all flue-cured stem blend for ESS,
but did produce some burley/flue-cured blend materials.
RJR built and operated a nominal 1000 Lb/Hr production line from 1998 to 2003. A single expander pilot
line was also built to support process development and external sales. Dickinson Legg was brought in to
market and build the equipment for outside sales. Plans are to transfer the pilot line to DIMON to provide
support for Dickinson Legg sales and marketing.
Objectives / Benefits ofTechnology:
The ESS process can produce an extremely high filling power material. It is especially useful in
processing short or small stems when a recon process is not available. These materials are useful in
producing high filling power value blends to produce low tobacco rod weight products.
ESS is also believed to improve the smoking characteristic of most stems. The relatively high processing
temperature removes some volatile materials and promotes production of thermal degradation products
from other compounds that occur in stems. Benefits include increased flavor from thermal processing
and smoother, milder taste. It is also believed to reduce "stemmy" attributes in smoke of many stem
materials.

SUBJECT: Revision of Filling Capacity Targets for G19-19 and G19-27 (Time Extension)
SUMMARY/BACKGROUND: Due to recent changes in leafi inventories, DIET filling capacity
levels on G19-19 and G19-27 expanded tobaccos have increased. The current CFC
specifications for these blends have targets of 760, with ship limits of 720 and 800 (+/- 40). Due
to process limitations (the inability to lower sublimator heat due to Forsyth County
Environmental Affairs Department permitting), the DIET process has consistently produced
these blends at the upper limit of 800. Projections of leaf inventory for 4Q 2000 and 2001
suggest that this trend will continue.
RECOMMENDATION: Implement temporary filling capacity specifications of 780 target,
with a ship limit range of 740-820 (+/- 40), pending reassessment of permanent specification in 4
months. Product moisture specifications will remain unchanged.
RISK ASSESSMENT: Projections ofl leafinventories may change beyond 2001. The risk to
finished cigarette is minimal.
REVIEWER COMMENTS: The permit for DIET can be revised so that incinerator/sublimator
temperatures can be lowered. This will take 3-4 months and $20-25 K of stack testing. Also,
there may be some modifications that could be done to lower sublimator temperature while
maintaining incinerator temperature to permit conditions. Recommend that we pursue a study
that would allow DIET to control filling capacity without impacting the permit conditions. Don

A proposal to re-introduce scrap from DIET back into G-19-5 has been requested = a memo
from R H. Laurence is attached. It is estimated that 212,000 lbs. of+18 scrap could be
reclaimed annually, for a savings of$130,200/yr. These are DIET expanded materials which
fall out of the main product stream,
This would involve taking scrap from DIET pans and vacuum to PRO for screening to reclaim
the material which rides the 18 mesh screen, then re-introducing it into DIET. Blend-back
would be done upstairs in DIET in the Blend-Back Feeder. The plant needs the option of
blending back as scrap and time are available. A maximum of 1500 Ibs. of+18 scrap would
be added to a 30,000 lb. blending bulker for a maximum 5% level into G-19-5 only. Average
inclusion would be only 1.2% (212,000 Ib/yr of+18 Scrap into 18 million Ib/yr ofG-19-5).
The impact to the product would be minimal for either average or maximum inclusion.
The exact breakdown oft the +18 scrap has not been determined, but a reasonable estimate
would be 70% +14, 30% -14. Product impact would then be as follows for an average 1.2%

THE WINSTON "NO BULL" INTERCEPT PROCESS
(CONTINUED)
Booth Agents
Booth agents wlll check ID to confirm smoker Is 21 years of age or older
Booth agents will check ID to ensure the photo looks like the 21+ smoker.
Booth agents will check to ensure that intercept card has been completed.
Booth agents will check to ensure each 21+ smoker has a pack of cigarettes.
All packs must not be complimentary, have at least one unsmoked cigarette
and it must match the brand on the pack. Also mark the 21+ smoker's pack
with a marker.(Important to minimize fraud)
Booth agents will photograph ID and intercept card. Military ID's must have a
picture taken of both sides. First the photo side. Second, Cross (X) over the
redemption card and photograph the backside of the ID.
Booth agents will return ID to 21+ smoker.
Give the 21+ smoker the gift bag and the carton of WINSTON.
Stamp the 21+ smokers left hand with the stamp.
Emphasize that WINSTONI is the only leading brand with 100% First Cut
Tobacco, no Additives and no Sheet (no reprocessed sheet tobacco made
from scraps). Because 100% tobacco naturally tastes better, No Bull.
Winston Greeter
There must be a Greeter present at the booth at all times during execution.
Greeters must check all Age Verification Forms for accuracy and
completeness. All questions must be answered, date of birth is correct,
address is correct, and consumer has signed the form.
Greeter will also double check ID's and make sure everyone in line has a
completed Age Verification Form and a pack of cigarettes.
Greeter is to help manage the flow and direction of the line at the booth.
Security Guards
There must be Security Guards at each booth at all times during execution.
Security Guards must verify each smoker is 21 years of age or older with a

SUBJECT:
Reprocessing of Speculative Offshore Tobaccos
OBJECTIVE:
Bring Tobaccos back into Specification for Stem Content
BACKGROUND: A purchase from dealers resulted in an available inventory of flue cured and
burley strip tobaccos at favorable pricing on an as is basis. Subsequent QA and Dealer data on
these tobaccos revealed that approximately 4 million pounds exceeded either the total or the
objectionable stem limit for lot averages of2.71 and .5% respectively. In order to use these
tobaccos processing is required to bring them within specification.
RECOMMENDATION: Process 4 million lbs of off spec tobaccos at Brook Cove to meet total
and objectionable stem specification.
RISK ASSESSMENT: Failure to process could increase stem complaints among consumers.
There will be a strip yield decrease estimated to be between 20 to 30% as well as a degradation in
strip size. Most ofthe loss will be recovered as either scrap and/or stem yield.
COST/BENEFIT: This will allow the Company to use 4 million pounds oftobacco that it owns
at a cost of .0155 per lb processing cost or about n S 62,000. All of the tobaccos to be
processed are Value tobaccos. None ofthe lots are preminum.

SUBJECT: STRATEGY FOR SHORTS SURPLUS
BRIEF SUMMARY: Cigarette shorts are utilized only in Savings segment products
(except MORE Menthol, NOW Menthol pre-BPU). Uncut tobaccos (UTI) are used
exclusively in Premium brands. Advantages of UTI include regulated recipes,
consistent inclusion rates and absence of paper, foil and other packaging
contaminants. Plant infeed systems are designed to feed either shorts or UTI at
rates between 3% and 12%. Premium Business Units have issues surrounding
reinstatement of shorts into full price brands.
The latest update to the company's Operating Plan indicates that a surplus of shorts is
likely for 1995 and following years. One option to address this surplus would be to
enlarge the final shorts screen (currently an 18 mesh) to generate fewer shorts.
However, particle size testing has shown no product quality benefits at sizes up to 10
mesh.
The initial impact of this surplus began to occur in October of 1994. Management of
Brands R&D and Engineering/Operations met at this time and agreed to implement the
following short term procedure.
PROPOSAL: It is recommended that the following shorts usage strategies be adopted
until further testing has been completed:
Continue use of shorts in savings only (post BPU) and current excess
inventory of shorts should be redirected to G7.
Once excess inventory has been stabilized, direct market returns to G7 except
in periods of low shorts inventory.
OBJECTIVE: The objective of this proposal is to manage tobacco materials in a
manner that preserves product quality in the most cost efficient manner.

SUBJECT: Product Acceptance-Suggestion/Vision Quest/In House Changes
OBJECTIVE: Ensure thorough review of process changes
BACKGROUND: On March 3, 1994 procedure note 94-3R was issued by the Product
Acceptance Committee. It stated that plant efficiency changes that could alter the quality of
finished product, such as detector setting changes and waste stream addition changes require PAC
approval. Any change in the fate of a waste stream will require PAC approval.
RECOMMENDATION:
1. Effective immediately, any ideas, suggestions, or Vision Quest ideas recommended for
adoption that reintroduces product in the process at Whitaker Park and/or Tobaccoville, will
be reviewed and, ift necessary forwarded for approval by the Product Acceptance committee
prior to Suggestion Committee Approval.
2. In house modification or decisions out of the realm of suggestions/Vision Quest by area
departments to reintroduce product in the process, be reviewed by the Making and Packing or
Primary waste teams prior to implementation. The chairman ofthe PACis represented on
both committees.
3. Suggestion programs in R&D, Tobacco Processing, Manufacturing and Engineering be
notified of this policy so their ideas will also go through this process. Kathi Long, overall
coordinator of suggestions has been notified so all suggestions will comply with this policy.
4. Define a general guideline for acceptable materiakas being free offoreign matter, mold,
damage, oil, or grease. It must have a +22 particle size, same composition, and comparable
moisture as its point of addition. This is the minimum criteria for review consideration.

SUBJECT: 25 cpi for DIET Blends
OBJECTIVE:
Improve Cigarette Rod Integrity
BACKGROUND:
As part of rod integrity studies, tests were run on Now 100 Regular and Menthol with
DIET blends produced at 25 cpi. Previous testing of DIET blend at 25 cpi vs. 30 cpi
showed a reduction in G19-7 fines of6.5%, finished cigarette fines of 2.6%, and no
significant difference in product machinability.
The results of this latest test can be summarized as follows (cigarette and reject data
are attached):
Diet was able to meet product specifications while decreasing fines significantly.
Percent longs, middlings and fines improved significantly for both NOW 100 and
NOW 100 Menthol blends using 25 cpi G19-19 versus 30 cpi G19-19.
Percent good ends, bad ends and Borgwaldt improved significantly for the NOW
100 blend using 25 cpi G19-19.
Percent good ends and bad ends improved directionally for the NOW 100 Menthol
blend using 25 cpi G19-19.
Borgwaldt became worse directionally for theNOW 100 Menthol blend using 25 cpi
G19-19.
Firecone fallout and Ash quality for 25 and 30 cpi were exceptional.

SUBJECT:
Drum Scrap Reclalm for G-7
OBJECTIVE: Reduce waste in primary operations
DISCUSSION:
Authorization was approved for $200,000 to install a "Truck Dryer" in C&D at
Tobaccoville. This dryer (approx. size 10' x 71 x 10' high) will be used to salvage wet
tobacco scrap removed from the casers and conditioning drums in Primary during clean
up.
Plant data shows there is 405,270 Ibs. of wet tobacco scrap that can be salvaged.
Presently, this product is sent to the landfill. On a dry basis, this converts to 110,528
Ibs./yr. of useable product. It is proposed to send this product to G-7 for use as a raw
material. This will result in savings of $84,000/yr. based on 76 cents/lb. with an ROI of
26.1% (business case calculations.)
Installation of the dryer will be considered a new emissions source and an Air Toxic
review was required. This process Is complete.
Alternatives Considered
Samples of Wet Drum Scrap were sent to R&D and dried In the Pilot Plant's Sergeant
Tray Dryer. Samples of the redried leaf were then sent to TOX and Tobacco
Processing. All evaluations were favorable.
Two options were considered for recycling the drum scrap:
1. Inclusion in Primary FBS: Careful considération was given to this option for adding
the redried leaf back to the Process. Samples were used to make cigarettes at 1;
10 & 50% inclusion rates. Because of certain quality considerations, Brands R&D
rejected this option at this time.
2. Raw Material for G-7 Infeed: This option was considered and approved by the
Primary Waste Committee and Tobacco Processing and felt to have a minimum
potential for affecting quality of our product.

SUBJECT:
Reprocessing of Speculative offshore Tobaccos
OBJECTIVE:
Bring Tobaccos back into Specification for Stem Content
BACKGROUND: A purchase from dealers resulted in an available inventory offlue cured and
burley strip tobaccos at favorable pricing on an as is basis. Subsequent QA and Dealer data on
these tobaccos revealed that approximately 4 million pounds exceeded either the total or the
objectionable stem limit for lot averages of2.71 and .5% respectively. In order to use these
tobaccos processing is required to bring them within specification.
RECOMMENDATION: Process 4 million lbs of off spec tobaccos at Brook Cove to meet total
and objectionable stem specification.
RISK ASSESSMENT: Failure to process could increase stem complaints among consumers.
There will be a strip yield decrease estimated to be between 20 to 30% as well as a degradation in
strip size. Most ofthe loss will be recovered as either scrap and/or stem yield.
COST/BENEFIT: This will allow the Company to use 4 million pounds of tobacco that it owns
at a cost of .0155 per lb processing cost or about m $ 62,000. All oft the tobaccos to be
processed are Value tobaccos. None of the lots are preminum.

SUBJECT: +18 MESH DIET RECLAIM
BRIEF SUMMARY: Approximately 708,000 pounds of G19 (DIET) scrap are generated
annually. Currently, this material is used as scrap in the G7 process.
PROPOSAL: Itis recommended that the following procedure be adopted for
disposition of G19 scrap:
Ship material to #2-1 PRO for screening on #1 sieve line.
Reclaim the portion of material retained on the 18 mesh screen for reblend
into G19-5 at the DIETfacility. This fraction is estimated to comprise 30%-35%
of the total amount.
Continue to direct the remaining material that passes the 18 mesh to G7.
OBJECTIVE: Adoption of this proposal should result in an annualized savings of
between $125,000 - $150,000 due to yield improvement.
RISK ASSESSMENT: There is no indication of any product risk as a result of
implementing this proposal. The average inclusion level of the reblend is
approximately 1.2% and does not displace lamina like the majority of other savings
proposals. For these reasons there is no reasonable risk to taste or performance
properties of finished product. Currently, G19 contains between 18%-29% pass 20
mesh material. Therefore, the addition of the +18 mesh material should have no impact
on rod integrity.

custom retails will need to notify McLane to lower their retail appropriately for their stores or
submit retail markdowns with each invoice. Effective close of business Aug. 29, 1999, the
retails need to be increased back to the appropriate retail.

1. Transfer 1 mL of cach calibration standard to autosampler vials and analyze
by GC/MS.
2. Obtain Extracted Ion Chromatograms for m/z 252 (BAP) and m/z 264 (BAP-
d12) from the Total Ion Chromatogram.
3. Integrate the area under these extracted ions.
4. Calculate the Response Factor (RF) as follows:
RF=((Arca IBAM/ Concentrationgar)). / (Area [BAP-d12] / Concentration [BAP-d12] )3
5. A typical plot ofi individual Response Factors is shown in Figure 1.
6. The Response Factor used for quantitation is the average of the individual
Response Factors.
B. Sample Analysis
1. The samples were analyzed in a computer generated random order.
2. The puffing parameters were 45 mL puff volume with 2 sec. puff duration
once every 30 sec. A strip of adhesive tape blocked 50 % oft the ventilation
holes.
3. Non-filter cigarettes were smoked to a 23 mm butt length and filter cigarettes
were smoked to a butt length that equals tipping paper +3 mm or 23 mm
whichever is longer.
4. The cigarettes were conditioned and smoked as specified in ISO 3402.
5. Weigh and record the weight of a conditioned Cambridge pad.
6. Collect the mainstream smoke from 10 conditioned cigaretles on the weighed
Cambridge pad.
7. Re-weigh the Cambridge pad and record weight for calculation ofTPM.
8. Add 10 LL ofinternal standard solution (25 ppm BAP-d12) to the Cambridge
pad.
9. Replace the 100 mL sample flask that came with the micro steam distillation
apparatus with a 500 mL round bottom using the 24/40 (outer) x 14/35 (inner)
adapter.
10. Replace the 10: mL solvent flask that came with the micro steam distillation
apparatus with a 25 mL pear shaped flask.
11. Place the smoke pad in the sample flask ofthe SDE apparatus. Add 250 mL
water, 30 g. sodium chloride and several boiling chips.
12. Place 15 mL methylene chloride in the solvent flask ofthe SDE apparatus
with several boiling chips.
13. Boil both flasks for five hours.
14. Concentrate the methylene chloride extract to approximately 1 mL under a
stream of nitrogen at room temperature.

Filter Type (B&W)
The composition of the filter is determined by visual examination of the removed

Filter Type (Lorillard)
Filter type is determined by visual inspection.

Filter type is determined through visual or chemical techniques. After outer
papers are removed, a visual examination is conducted. If a visual determination
cannot be made, the sample is placed in acetone or sulfuric acid. Cellulose
acetate dissolves in acetone and paper dissolves in sulfuric acid. Only 1
cigarette is required per determination.
Filter Type (R.J. Reynolds)
Filter type is determined through visual inspection. The cigarette filter is visually
examined. An average of five cigarettes are examined per sample. Filters are
categorized according to the following types: cellulose acetate, concentric paper
and recessed charcoal.

Tip Dilution (B&W)
CTS is a combined method for the determination of cigarette weight,
circumference, ventilation, pressure drop, and cigarette hardness. For the
purpose of this study, only circumference and ventilation are reported. Ventilation

volume of air exiting the cigarette's tipping is sensed by the pressure differential
in the tipping region, which is isolated through a series of inflatable latex bobbins.
Ventilation results are measured to the tenth of a percent. Upon completion of
the analysis of the 20 cigarettes, individual data points, as well as mean,
standard deviation, and coefficient of variance is exported by the CTS.

V. Procedure
A. Cigarette Conditioning
Cigarettes are conditioned at 75+2°F and 60+2% RH for at least 48 hours, but no
more than 10 days. For analyses using Massachusetts smoking parameters, 50% of
the ventilation holes on the cigarette are blocked using a strip of transparent tape 1 ,
before mechanical smoking. Tape is applied without regard to the cigarette seam.
B. Snecifications for the Collection of Mainstream Smoke
All samples are smoked in a room conditioned at 75+2°F and 60+2% RH. The
subgroups are those stated in the study protocol 1 - The cigarettes are smoked to a
butt length of3 mm plus the tipping paper for filtered cigarettes and 23 mm for
non-filtered cigarettes. The cigarettes are positioned sO that the stringing ofthe
machine is practical, e.g. 100 mm cigarettes are placed next to 85 mm not 70 mm
cigarettes. No brand is smoked twice on the same port of the smoking machine.
The filter pad and holder are weighed together, before and after smoking, for the
determination of TPM. Puff counts are recorded.
1. Massachusetts Parameters
The Phipps and Bird smoking machine 4 is programmed to take a: 210.2
second puff of 4510.5 mL volume every 3011 seconds. A 44 mm filter pad
holder, with a pad and a dental dam, holds the cigarette in place. Three
cigarettes per replicate and 20 replicates per brand are smoked. Replicates
ofl Philip Morris Monitor 16 (Monitor) and replicates of blanks ofpuffing
room air are smoked daily.

First Quarter Highlights
(excluding food restructuring-related costs in 1999 and initial, upfront tobacco

Operating company contribution down 21% to $577 million
Cash net income down 32% to $208 million
Net sales up 7% to $4.22 billion
RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. (NYSE:RN) today announced results for the first quarter
cnded March 31, 1999. Net income per diluted common share was $.24 for the quarter,
down 54 percent from net income per diluted common share of $.52 reported in the first
quarter of 1998. Nct income for the quarter was $83 million, down
54 percent from nct income of $179 million in the first quarter of 1998. Results exclude
restructuring-related expenses of $15 million at the food business in 1999 ($7 million
afler-tax, net of minority intcrest or $.02 per diluted common share) and initial, upfront
tobacco scttlement-related costs in 1998 of $312 million ($199 million after-tax or $.62
per diluted common share).
On the same basis, operating company contribution (operating income before
amortization oftrademarks and goodwill) for the first quarter was $577 million, down 21
percent from $732 million for the first quarter of 1998. Net sales for the 1999 first
quarter were
$4.22 billion, a 7 percent increasc compared to net sales of $3.95 billion in the 1998
quarter.
"Nabisco is showing great progress, - said Steven F. Goldstone, chairman and chief
cxccutive officer of RJR Nabisco. "Fundamental changes made during the past 15
months are resulting in a return to top-line growth in the U.S. biscuit business. Volume,
salcs and sharc gains are once again evident in the domestic cookie and cracker business
as well as in other U.S. food product lines."

Dr. Charles Green announced that, as of this meeting, he was stepping down as convenor
for this group. He recommended that Dr. Michael Ogden be named new convenor. This
recommendation was supported unanimously by attending task force members. The
Scientific Commission has been requested to confirm Dr. Ogden's appointment.
After reviewing the Scientific Commission's definitions for task force and sub-group, it is
our belief that the ETS Task Force should rightly be deemed the ETS Sub-Group. The
Scientific Commission has been requested to confirm this name change.
In an effort to hasten progress, the ETS Sub-Group desires to hold a 1/2 day session
during the Vienna Meeting of the. Smoke & Technology Groups. The secretary of the
Smoke Group, Maria Elmano Rocha, has been requested to make appropriate
arrangements.
The ETS Sub-Group will conduct a collaborative study of the ETS methods for
gravimetric RSP, UVPM, FPM, solanesol, nicotine and 3-ethenylpyridine. Fourteen
laboratories will participate. Dr. Ogden leads a group consisting of Barrie Frost, and J.-J.
Piadé to organize the study,

made it the logical home for this work and not a new task force. Our initial project is to

Weight methods. Cigarette Tobacco Weight is calculated by subtracting
NonTobacco weight from cigarette weight mean. Results are reported as
mg/cigarette.
Tobacco Weight (Lorillard)
The weight of 30 cigarettes is recorded. The papers and filters of all 30
cigarettes are removed and weighed. The tobacco weight is calculated by
difference.
Tobacco Weight (Philip Morris)
Tobacco weight is determined using an indirect method. A group of 15
cigarettes is weighed and the composite weight recorded. The paper and filters
of the corresponding 15 cigarettes are then removed and weighed and the
composite weight recorded. The tobacco weight is calculated by difference. The
average tobacco weight per cigarette is obtained by dividing the difference by 15.
Results are reported in grams.
Tobacco Weight (R.J. Reynolds)
Tobacco weight is determined by slicing open the cigarette and gravimetrically
determining the weight of the tobacco to the nearest one-thousandth of a gram.
An average of five cigarette determinations are performed for each sample.
4. Cigarette Circumference
Cigarette Circumference (B&W)
A Filtrona CTS 400 with Automatic Hopper Loader (AHL) is used for the
circumference determination. Samples consist of 20 cigarettes, with each
cigarette being tested individually. The AHL transports individual cigarettes to
the testing station. The second module determines cigarette circumference by
the linear displacement of a tape gauge that encircles the cigarette.
Circumference results are measured to the one hundredth of a millimeter.
Cigarette Circumference (Lorillard)
The calibration of the Filtrona CTS-400 circumference module is verified before
each use by measuring the 25.00 mm standard. If the measurement error is
more than 25.00+0.01 mm, the module is recalibrated and the recalibration is
verified. The samples are loaded into the Filtrona CTS-400 and are fed
automatically through the test station. The cigarettes fall into the catch pan at the
bottom of the test station after the appropriate tests have been performed.

Research atl.T.C.-I.T.L.D.
T.S. SUBRAMANIAM took the opportunity oft the Golden Jubilee (50th anniversary) of the
Research Department ofIndia Tobacco Company to present its history and achievements.
Founded in 1949, the Research Department is active in Agronomy, Plant Breeding, Plant
Protection, Plant Physiology, Product Development, Chemistry and Post-Harvest Hygiene.
Training is also a major mission of this entity.
A major development that took place since the early 70's is the introduction of tobacco on
Northern Light Soils, with new varieties being developed and gradually improved. This area
now grows flavour grades.
Over the years, ITC-ILTD has achieved excellent results in energy, water and soil
conservation, while increasing yields drastically, from 660 kg/ha in 1950 to 1750 kg/ha in
1999.
CORESTA Documentation
François JACOB was requested at the SC meeting held in January to consider the setting up
of a task force to reflect on the general question of the CORESTA documentation.
Since January, a few visits and contacts were made, and an experimental CORESTA web-
site (www.coresta.org) was created. The general question ofthe CORESTA documentation
can be seen from various angles:
Contents: what exactly is expected from CORESTA? Would the American Conferences or
Universities be interested in a common work with CORESTA?
Media:
paper, CD, web-site. What information on what medium?
Access:
this mainly concerns the web-site: should it be fully open, or partially/totally
restricted to CORESTA members?
The Scientific Commission decided to create a working group on this matter, with the
objective of defining clear, if not final, propositions by the next Congress in Lisbon.
This working group will be composed of Sergio BREMM, Brian SMEETON, Richard
BAKER, Takeshi SAKAKI, Yves SAINT-JALM, Martin WARD and François JACOB.

R&DM, PSYMEM 96-001

Eclipse prototypes 6-110A, 6-110B and 6-117C were determined relative to Marlboro Lights 85 Box
cigarettes (REF). The study was run in the Bldg. 611-9 environmental test chamber #1. Analytes
determined included RSP, nicotine, 3-ethenylpyridine, CO, CO,, NO, NO,, NO,, total hydrocarbons
(FID).

GENERAL INFORMATION
PASSPORTS AND VISAS
All foreign visitors entering Great Britain must possess a valid passport (or identity card for
Nationals ofthe European Community).
You may also need a visa to enter Great Britain. Since visas vary according to purpose,
please enquire about the details at the British Embassy or Consulate in your country.
CURRENCY
The currency of Great Britain is the Pound Sterling (E), which is divided into 100 pence.
Foreign exchange facilities (usually called "Bureau de Change") are available at all the
London airports, London rail stations, many banks and travel agents.
Foreign exchange facilities are notavailable at The Grand Hotel - you should pay your hotel
bill by credit card, travellers' cheques (in sterling) or Sterling Cash.
CREDIT CARDS
Visa, Master Card, American Express and Diners Club are widely accepted at hotels,
department stores, shops and restaurants.
SHOPPING
In all major cities the shops are open from 09.00 until 17.30 hours, Monday to Saturday.
Many shops are also open on Sundays from 10.00 until 16.00 hours.
All goods sold in Great Britain include Value Added Tax (VAT) at 17.5%.
Many shops throughout the country operate a tax free scheme for overseas visitors. The store
will provide a form which should be completed at the time of purchase. Upon arrival at
Customs when yyou leave Great Britain, present the form and goods to the Customs Officer,
who will stamp the form certifying that the goods have been exported. You will then be
entitled to a refund ofVAT.
ELECTRICITY
The domestic electricity is 240 volts AC, 50 Hz. British-style plugs are used universally
(three pin, rectangular and fused).
WEATHER
The weather in England in mid October is difficult to predict, as it is throughout the year!
It is variable from day to day. In mid October it can range from sunny but cool (up to 12°C)
to wet and windy, Night time temperatures of about 5°C are likely.
For outdoors it is recommended that a showerproof coat is worn.
It starts to get dark at about 6.00 p.m.

AND MUTAGENICITY MARKET SURVEY
OBJECTIVE
The 1998 Market Survey of cigarette smoke chemistry and cigarette smoke condensate
mutagenicity was initiated to provide baseline data for market surveys, to provide additional
smoke chemistry data, and to examine the constancy ofthe smoke chemistry profile of
commercially marketed cigarettes over the period of 1995-2000. Chemistry data were published
(Swauger et al, 2002). However, due to resource conflicts, the mutagenicity portion off the study
was not completed, so that data from assays of only 28 brands are available (only one of6 FF
menthol brands, none of 5 FFLT menthol brands, and neither of2 ULT menthol brands were
run). Thus, results from this study were not published either internally or externally.
Nevertheless, mutagenicity data from 28 brands from this study are available and were analyzed
at the request of Dr. David Doolittle to investigate whether 'tar' from full flavor-low 'tar' (FFLT
or 'Light") cigarettes was more mutagenic than 'tar' from full flavor (FF) cigarettes. Analysis
was performed in an attempt to provide additional understanding from these data even though the
survey was incomplete and not specifically designed to answer this question.
SUMMARY
Data from the 1998 smoke chemistry and mutagenicity market surveyincluded mutagenicity
measurements of cigarette smoke condensate (CSC) from 28 cigarette brands from the U.S.
market. Assays were run using both strains TA98 and TA100. Using the determination of
revertants/mg 'tar' and the 'tar' yield obtained by smoking each cigarette in the R&D smoke lab
(FTC method), mutagenicity in units of revertants per cigarette was calculated as well. For our
purposes, data for cigarettes in the ultra-light category (generally < 6 mg. 'tar' per the FTC
method) were excluded from analysis, so that results from assays of 13 FF brands (generally >>

THERMAL STUDY OF TOTAL PARTICULATE MATTER OF 1R5F
CIGARETTES
OBJECTIVE:
The purpose of this study was to determine the stability and weight loss of total
particulate matter of 1R5F cigarette sample.
SUMMARY:
A sample of total particulate matter (TPM) of the 1R5F cigarettes was obtained by
electrostatic precipitation of cigarette smoke. Cigarettes were smoked with one 35 mL
puff of 2-second duration taken each 60 seconds. The sample was analyzed for thermal
property by the thermogravimetric (TG) technique. A small amount (20 mg) of the
sample was heated in the presence of air. The temperature was programmed from
ambient temperature (24°C) to 230°C at 2.5°C/min and held for 16 minutes.
Thermogravimetric analysis shows weight loss (evaporation/decomposition) for the 1R5F
cigarette sample was 51%.
STATUS:
This study is complete.

THERMAL STUDY OF TOTAL PARTICULATE MATTER OF 1R5F
CIGARETTES
OBJECTIVE:
The purpose of this study was to determine the stability and weight loss of total
particulate matter of 1R5F cigarette sample.
SUMMARY:
A sample of total particulate matter (TPM) of the IR5F cigarettes was obtained by
electrostatic precipitation of cigarette smoke. Cigarettes were smoked with one 35 mL
puff of 2-second duration taken each 60 seconds, The sample was analyzed for thermal
property by the thermogravimetric (TG) technique. A small amount (20 mg) of the
sample was heated in the presence of air. The temperature was programmed from
ambient temperature (24°C) to 230°C at 2.5°C/min and held for 16 minutes.
Thermogravimetric analysis shows weight loss (evaporation/decomposition) for the IR5F
cigarette sample was 51%.
STATUS:
This study is complete.

HEALTH EFFECTS AND FIRST AID
INHALATION: Acute exposure may cause respiratory and throat irritation. High vapor
concentration may cause central nervous system depression with headache, dizziness and
drowsiness. Chronic exposure may cause nystagmus, lymphocytosis and unconsciousness.
FIRST AID: Remove from exposed area to fresh air. If breathing has stopped, perform
artificial respiration. Get medical attention.
SKIN CONTACT: Acute and chronic exposure may cause irritation, dryness of skin and
dermatitis due to defatting action of the liquid. FIRST AID: Remove contaminated clothing and
wash affected area with soap and large amounts of water. Get medical attention.
EYE CONTACT: Direct contact may cause redness and irritation. Chronic exposure may cause
conjunctivitis. FIRST AID: Wash eyes immediately with large amounts of water. Get medical
attention.
INGESTION: The initial symptoms in massive dose (over 100 mL in a single dose) are those of
alcohol intoxication. These symptoms soon progress to vomiting, cyanosis, headache, tachypnea,
tachycardia, hypotension, pulmonary edema, muscle tenderness, stupor, anuria, prostration, and
unconsciousness. Hypoglycemia may occur. Death may occur due to respiratory failure or
pulmonary edema. Patients who have prolonged coma or convulsions may have irreversible
brain damage. Massive doses may cause intravascular hemolysis. FIRST AID: If victim is
conscious, immediately give large amounts of water. Induce vomiting. Get medical attention
immediatcly.
REACTIVITY
INCOMPATIBILITIES: Propylene glycol reacts vigorously with oxidizing agents. Hazardous
polymerization will not occur. When heated propylene glycol decomposes to form peroxides and
propionaldehyde.
SPILL PROCEDURES
Wear protective cquipment and approved respiratory cquipment. Absorb with sand or other
noncombustible absorbent material and place into containers for disposal by approved methods.
PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT
Normal laboratory protective clothing, splash proof glasses and impervious gloves are adequate.
Do NOT wcar contact lcnscs when working with this chemical.

The noticeable improvement in the Company's export performance during the year is visible from the
above data. Proactive measures and various initiatives to boost export performance have been yielding
encouraging results. While cigarette exports in terms of value were higher by 84%, the unmanufactured
tobacco export registered a significant increase of 24% over the preceding year. Cut tobacco exports
increased by 10% over the previous year.
For cigarette and cut tobacco exports, the Company is actively looking at new markets and has recruited
new managers for prospecting business in new geographies. Apart from continuous focus on CIS and
Russian Federation, efforts are on to increase number of markets in the current year. The major regions
where the Company is currently exporting include South East Asia, Africa, Middle East and Latin America.
For unmanufactured tobacco exports, the measures taken by the Company include broadening the list of
buyers and opening of new markets for direct exports in Middle East and Europe. With a view to enhance
fruitful business association, customers and agents are being invited to see the Company's operations
and infrastructure which has been widely appreciated.
Tea exports, however, registered negative growth mainly on account of loss of business in Kazakhstan due
to their Government raising import duty on packet tea rendering the imports unviable. Eforts are being
made to forge new international contacts, attain cost and quality efficiencies and meet Multi Original Blend
Standard requirements of International Buyers.
During thet first quarter of current financial year, the Company has achieved export turnover of Rs. 80 crore
which is lower than Rs. 102 crore achieved in the corresponding period of last year. The Company is
making all out efforts to achieve higher export turnover as compared to the preceding year and hopes to
make up in the remaining part of the year to be able to attain double digit growth as in the past.
Chewing Products
With a view to achieve its growth objectives, the Company has entered into Chewing Products category
with the launch of Pan Masala brand "Pan Vilas". This brand has set the benchmark for the Pan Masala
Industry in many ways. Firstly, it is free of Magnesium Carbonate, a banned substance and replaces
the same with a natural alternate and is made compliant to the stringent requirements of PFA rules.
Secondly, itis manufactured in a state-of -the-art plant setup at Baramati, near Pune, which employs some
of the world's best food processing technologies - imported multi-stage cleaning unit which removes
finest of impurities, cutting edge Supari roasting unit which ensures uniform crispness of supari and high
speed packaging machines. Finally, the sales and marketing strategies are based on in-depth consumer,
competitor and trade understanding, which has raised the bar in the manner this category has been
traditionally marketed.

INDUSTRY STRUCTURE AND DEVELOPMENT:
The Industry posted a 3% growth in volumes over the previous year. However, your Company's volumes grew by 7% compared to
last year. Further, in the economy non-filtered segment, where your Company mainly operates, with thrust in the rural market, our
market share has increased to 36% for the financial year 2003-04 compared to 31% last year.
Inspite of challenges faced by the Industry in terms of high state level taxes in form of Luxury and/ or Entry tax; smuggled
Cigarettes finding their way into the domestic market and with the implementation of the 'Cigarettes and Other Tobacco Products
(Prohibition of Advertisement & Regulation of Trade & Commerce, Production, Supply & Distribution) Act, 2003' effective from
1st May, 2004, your Company is striving to increase its sales volumes and market share, especially in its core markets.
REHABILITATION PACKAGE:
The rehabilitation package as approved by the Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) vide its order dated
16/12/2002 is being implemented satisfactorily. The Management Committee is monitoring the progress of the scheme.
FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE WITH RESPECT TO OPERATIONAL PERFORMANCE
The Sales Revenue of your Company during the year was at Rs. 30746. 16 lacs as against Rs. 32840.94 lacs in the previous
year, showing a decline of 6.38%. However, the profit after tax for the year increased by around 57% from Rs. 475.22 lacs in the
previous year to Rs.747.72 lacs this year. The export revenue generated during the year 2003-04 was Rs. 2430.03 lacs.
This performance has been fuelled inter alia, by various planned new marketing initiatives bearing fruit, which has expanded
our consumer base apart from the several cost saving measures undertaken by your Company in its operations. Your
Company continues to have the single largest Brand in the mini cigarettes segment in the country, steadily adding to its market
share.
In view of the accumulated losses, your Directors are unable to recommend a dividend.
FIXED DEPOSIT:
There are no fixed deposit dues pending repayment by the Company. Interest free Contributions have been received from
Associates towards "Promoters' Contribution', as directed by the BIFR vide its order dated 16th December, 2002 approving the

1.
THE COMPANY'S GOVERNANCE PHILOSOPHY
GHs Corporate Governance initiatives are devised for achieving basic objective ofwealth creation for the
benefit of all its stakeholders namely the shareholders, employees, business associates and the society at
large. The Company believes in giving its executives ample freedom to operate and secure the Company's
targetby putting in best of their efforts.
The Board of Directors is primarily responsible for prot tecting and enhancing shareholders value besides
fulfilling the Company's obligations towards other stakeholders. The role of the Board of Directors is to
provide strategic superintendence over the Company's management. The day to day management of the
Company is vested in the managerial personnel and sufficient authority is delegated at different operating
levels. Delegation of authority in the operating people helps generation of creativity and innovation. This
also helps in harnessing pot tential of employees to the best advantage ofthe Company.

Board ofDirectors is nine outofwhich five are non-executive Directors. The Chairman of the Board is a non-
executive directorand the minimum requirementofone-third ofthe Board consisting ofindependent directors
is duly complied with. The non-executive directors ofthe Company have already submitted theirdeclarations
affirming their status as independent directors as on March 31, 2010.

Company's Philosophy on Code of Corporate Governance
The Company firmly believes in and has consistently endeavoured to practice good Corporate Governance. It endeavours to
provide detailedi information on various issues concerning the Company's business and financial performance to the shareholders.
The spirit of Corporate Governance has prevailed in the Company and has influenced its decisions and policies. The Company
firmly believes in the values of transparency, professionalism and accountability in its dealings with its customers, suppliers,
lenders, employees and with every individual who comes in contact with the Company.
The following is the report on the status and progress made on major aspects of Corporate Governance:
I
Board of Directors
At the beginning of the financial year, the Company had seven Directors on its Board, of which three were executive Directors,
i.e. one Managing Director and two Whole-time Directors; one Nominee Director appointed by the Board for Industrial and
Financial Reconstruction (B.I.F.R.) and three non-executive directors. Shri J.P. Khetan was reappointed as Managing Director
of the Company with effect from 1st August, 2003. Shri Bharat B. Merchant was appointed as Director of the Company in the
Annual General Meeting dated 24th September, 2003. Shri N.V.. Joshi, Director of the Company resigned as such on 21st October,
2003. Shri A.K. Joshi was appointed as Additional Director of the Company on 21st October, 2003. Shri Chandra Shankar
ceased to be a Special Director under an order issued by the B.I.F.R. with effect from 5th July, 2004.
As a result of the above changes, the present strength of the Board is six Directors, consisting of three executive Directors and
three non-executive Directors. All the six Directors are independent Directors.

GODFREY PHILLIPS
CORPORATE SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITY
Godfrey Phillips Bravery Awards, a resolve that began in 1990, is today a nationwide movement. it salutes
and celebrates individual acts of bravery and brings to light today's unsung heroes, who work against
social evils and champion the cause of transformation of society at large, inspiring many more. The
national award function was a prestigious event attended by several famous personalities, and widely
covered by the media. The television commercial created for the award function won the coveted
"Abby" award.
Your Company realizes that the first step towards women's emancipation is to impart them with the skills
they need to pursue a vocation and gain financial independence. Therefore, in close collaboration with
some renowned NGOS, it initiated several major projects for underprivileged women, under the aegis of
"Amodini", a women's empowerment initiative. These projects strive to provide primary and secondary
education to underprivileged women, conduct vocational training for women, aid in higher skill and
product development that help them create premium products out of traditional goods. Under a project
called "Gift for Good", products made by economically challenged women were promoted to
organizations and individuals as social gifts. Over 1000 women would have benelited from Amodini
initiatives during the year.
The Company has been awarded the Gold Award in FMCG sector for Outstanding Achievement in
Environment Management and Silver Award for Safety by Greentech Foundation.
CONSERVATION OF ENERGY
During the year under report, following measures were taken by the Company for conservation of
energy :
1. Screw Air Chiller was installed in the Making Department airconditioning plant, thus saving 480
units/day.
2. Installed power factor panel to improve the power factor to 0.99.
3. implemented server virtualization and precision cooling at the information technology data centre to
reduce energy consumption.
TECHNOLOGICAL ABSORPTION, ADOPTION AND INNOVATION
The measures initiatedlimplemented during the year under report are:
1. Installation and commissioning of fhigh speed (600 packs/minute) cigarette packing machine resulting
into improved productivity and product quality.
2. Installation and commissioning of 'on- -line laser perforation unit on cigarette making machine to help
improve product quality.
3. Installation and commissioning of 'double paper unit on cigarette making machine to reduce side
stream smoke of cigarettes.
4. Installation and commissioning of 'vertical slicer to improve consistency in quality parameters of
tobacco processing.
5. Installation and commissioning of new cigarette ripping machine to improve quality of process
addback.

PRESIDENT'S MESSAGE
Dear Shareholder,
It gives me great pleasure that in the last year your Company registered 11% growth from Rs 1295 crore last year to
Rs 1431 crore this year. Your Company's tobacco business continues to grow higher than the Industry growth of 6.3%.
A remarkable feat to achieve, against thel backdrop of increased marketing costs and additional excise duty of 5% levied
on top of last year's 10%. This achievement just goes to reiterate our belief in 'excelling through excellence'. The Board
of Directors of the company have recommended an all time high dividend of Rs 22.5 per equity share of Rs 10 each for
they year 2005-06.
At the beginning of 2005, we identified 20 areas where we could improve upon quality as well as reduce the cost of
production. We implemented the first wave of a sharply defined Six Sigma Programme in these areas and trained
9 Black Belts and 11 Green Belts to lead the initiative. We not only achieved annualised savings of approximately
Rs3 3.5 crore but were also able to improve quality of our products.
While we had decided to devote 2005-06 for building internal capabilities, the next year shall see' 'Six Sigma' being
implemented in virtually every aspect off the way Godfrey Phillips India operates and functions. Asl write to you, second
wave of the Six Sigma initiatives is being implemented with 12 Black Belts and 23 Green Belts being trained to lead
35 newly identified projects.
Your Company continues to look beyond profits and contributes substantially to the society from where it makes its
profits. While Godfrey Phillips Bravery, a 16y year old initiative was given the shape ofar national movement last year, this
yearl am happy to bring on board Ms Preity Zinta as the Godfrey Phillips Bravery Ambassador. Ms Preity Zinta will help
us take the message of bravery and selfless courage to the masses. Aiming to promote responsible smoking behaviour,
we launched another social initiative WHITE (acronym for We Honour the Importance of Tobacco Etiquette);
the Programme lays down avoluntary code for consumers of tobacco products and shall seek to promote a harmonious
co-existence between those who consume tobacco andt those who do not.
lam sure that Godfrey Phillips India shall continue to succeed even in the regulatory odds and continue to scale greater
growth year after year, just as it shall continue to look beyond profits to bring about a positive change for this planet
and its people.

SIGNIFICANT ACCOUNTING POLICIES
The financial statements are prepared under the historical cost convention in accordance with applicable
accounting standards and relevant presentational requirements of the Companies Act, 1956.
i)
Fixed assets and depreciation
Fixed assets are stated at cost of acquisition or construction less accumulated depreciation and
include interest on loans attributable to the acquisition of qualifying assets upto the date of their
commissioning.
No amortization is done in respect of leasehold land in view of the lease being perpetual.
Depreciation in the accounts is charged on the straight line method at the higher of the rates
prescribed under the Companies Act, 1956 or the accelerated rates determined based on their
useful lives as per technical estimates of the Management, and is calculated on a full year basis
on additions during the year and no depreciation is provided on assets deleted during the year.
Assets, other than items costing upto Rs. 5000 each, are depreciated upto 95% of their value
and 5% residual value is retained in the books.

ii)
Investments
Long term investments are stated at cost net of provision for diminution other than temporary, if
any. Current investments are stated at cost or fair value, whichever is lower.
iii)
Inventories
Inventories are valued at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower except stores and
spare parts which are valued at cost or under. The cost of raw materials, stores and spares and
traded goods is determined on moving weighted average cost basis. The cost of finished goods
and work-in-process is determined on standard absorption cost basis which approximates actual
costs. Absorption cost comprises raw materials cost, direct wages, appropriate share of production
overheads and applicable excise duty paid/payable thereon.
iv)
Revenue recognition
Sale of goods is recognised at the point of dispatch of goods to customers. Sales are inclusive
of excise duty where applicable but exclusive of sales tax/value added tax. Income from
investments is recognised on an accrual basis.

REPORT ON CORPORATE GOVERNANCE FOR THE THE YEAR ENDED MARCH 31, 2002
The Directors present the Company's Report on Corporate Governance.
1. THE COMPANY'S GOVERNANCE PHILOSOPHY
GPI's Corporate Governance initiatives are devised for achieving basic objective of wealth creation for the benefit of all its
stakeholders namely the shareholders, employees, business associates and the society at large. The Company believes in
giving its executives ample freedom to operate and secure the Company's target by putting in best of their efforts.
The Board of Directors is primarily responsible for protecting and enhancing shareholders' values besides fulfilling the
Company's obligations towards other stakeholders. The role of the Board of Directors is to provide strategic superintendence
over the Company's management. The day to day management of the Company is vested in the managerial personnel and
sufficient authority is delegated at different operating levels. Delegation of authority in the operating people helps generation
of creativity and innovation. This also helps in harnessing potential of employees to the best advantage of the Company.
2. BOARD OF DIRECTORS
i)
Composition
The Board of Directors of the Company consists of executive and non-executive directors and more than half of the
Board comprises of non-executive directors. The non-executive directors are independent professionals drawn from
amongst persons with experience in business law/finance. At present the total strength of the Board of Directors is nine
out of which five are non-executive Directors. The Chairman oft the Board is a non-executive director and the minimum
requirement of one-third of the Board consists of independent directors is duly complied with.

The Company firmly believes in and has consistently endeavoured to practice good Corporate Governance. It endeavours to provide detailed

non-executive directors.

executive independent Directors.

To continue to support low-dose Prempro and to set the stages for the introduction of new
non-hormonal products to treat vasomotor symptoms and osteoporosis, DesignWrite will
develop full-length review articles (2500-5000 words) to be published in peer-reviewed
journals, as well as abstracts and posters for scientific meetings. We will assist in
identifying external key experts in vasomotor symptoms and osteoporosis.

generated from the Asian-Pacific low-dose clinical trial in leading peer-reviewed
journals, as well as scientific meetings.
On an as needed basis, we will work with Wyeth in support of Women's Health Care
products in their development of response papers, modifications of existing manuscripts,

RJR INTEROFFICE MEMORANDUM
August 16, 1989
TO: Distribution
RE: Meeting Notes I NOW LN 90-C Simulation Test
Objective:
In support of NOW LN 90-C,* determine the following:
Relative nicotine reductions (single/double pass) by tobacco type;
Tobacco processing parameters;
Relative tobacco degradation;
Potential problems/adjustments needed in blending, tobacco processing
and/or cigarette making.
(*NOTE:
Older stabilization burley and flue-cured tobaccos were used to
simulate the physical condition of GLA tobaccos.)
Background:
Previous testing has indicated that denicotinization of various blend
components are necessary to achieve the target reduction of 90% in smoke
nicotine. The results of denicotinization with respect to both nicotine
removal degradation are not the same for all starting materials. This test
was conducted to uncover problems/investigate options for achieving the
target nicotine reduction while minimizing potential problems.
Evaluation:
Tobacco types used were: stabilization burley and flue-cured; G7-1;
standard TB blend. All tobaccos were denicotinized with two passes through
605; samples were taken for analyses after both the first and second
passes. (See Attachment 1). The test blend was the same as current NOW
100 with respect to % G-13, final top dressing and moisture. Differences
included: levels of various blend components; casing; cuts per inch (25
for test).
Cigarettes were made over three successive days at Whitaker Park on a
single Protos maker. A one-hole crescent design water tongue (5ml H20/min)
was used. Current NOW 100 Regular cigarette materials were used.
Summary of Results:
Current denic process is capable of achieving target reduction; single
pass probably sufficient.
As expected, not all starting materials processed the same through
denic with respect to nicotine removal, residual ammonia, fines. (See
Attachment 2).
Puffing location changed to 601; problems encountered at 63 with
5
tobacco slipping on feed conveyor (no cleats).
601 was able to cut to approximately 26 cpi; tobacco puffed well.

When you listen to a PowerPoint presentation about a topic in bullet
point form, there are two parts of the brain which are activated; the
Brocas's Area (1) and the Wernicke's area (2). These are simply the
language processing areas of the brain where words are turned into
meaning, but nothing else.
However, when we are being told a story not only are these
language centres in the brain activated but also the areas
of the brain associated with experiencing the story's
events come to life too.
For example, if the story includes an action such as
kicking or running, the motor cortex (3) of our brains
will light up. If the story has details such as
mentioning someone's "hands like
leather" our sensory response will
light up. The brain reacts as ifyou
were experiencing the story first
hand.
fig.2

the brain ofthelistener. In studies at Princeton University, thel brain activity ofa woman telling a story and her
listeners was monitored and as she told her story, her listener's brain activity went into sync with hers.
This means that writers have the ultimate power to influence others. With a
powerful and evocative story you can activate your reader's brains and make
them feel like they are experiencing it first-hand, influencing the emotions you
want them to feel.

Coralreefs are formed when tiny animals called Coral Polyps extract
minerals from the ocean and convert it into hard skeleton homes When
Coral Polyps die the limestone sheleton remains, This forms the
building blocks of a coral reef system.
Zooxanthellae algae assist in the process They live inside the coral's
cells and provide it with food and also its rich and vibrant colours
Coral cays are formed when coral skeletons, algae and other reef
creatures, sand and rubble are trapped by currents, wind and waves.
Over time the environment stabilises and a coralicay is established
About one thirdi of the coral cays on the Great Barrier Reef support

Koala
Koalas are nocturnal marsupials who reside in
Eucalypt forests. They consume around two
pounds of leaves a night, a diet that offers little
nutrition. Thus, koalas conserve as much energy
as possible and sleep around 18 hours a day. They
are not social animals, and only interact to mate.
Emu
Emus are Australia' 's largest bird, and
the second largest in the world after the
ostrich. These flightless birds are unique
to Australia and can grow to be up to
6.2 feet tall.
Wombat
Wombats are the second largest marsupial
(the Kangaroo being largest) but have the
largest brains of all marsupials. They're
smart animals who live below ground, and
often dig alternate exits from burrows when
traps have been placed at the entrances. They
compensate for bad vision with strong senses
of smell and hearing.

Although dingoes weigh only up to 60
pounds, they are the largest carnivores
in Australia. Evidence suggests they, were
brought to Australia by seafarers from
Asia about 4,500 years ago.
antaroo
Kangaroos live in groups of 5 to 40 individuals, called
"mobs". Kangaroos are fascinating animals who get
around by jumping orl bouncing, rather than walking.
A baby kangaroo, known as a joey, will live in its
mother's pouch for the first 6-8 months of life.
The wallaby, another famous Australian animal, is a
member of the kangaroo family.

that the first scientists to example them
believed it to be a hoax. The platypus can
be described as duck-billed, beaver-tailed,
and otter-footed. Female platypodes are
the only mammals to lay eggs rather than giving birth,
while male platypodes are the only venomous mammals.
Devil
Tasmanian -
Why called the "devil"? The Tasmanian
Devil is only about the size of a
housecat, but its aggressive nature
earned the animal its nasty name.
They're known for growling, hissing,
and even screaming. Though they fight with
their jaws agape, this expression can also
indicate joy or laughter.

HOW THE
UNITED STATES FARMS
654 million acres = pasture/range
More than 33% of U.S. land is used for pasture -by far the
largest land-use type in the contiguous 48 states. And nearly
25% of that land is administered by the federal government,
with most occurring in the West.
(The federal government manages livestock grazing on 158 million acres.)
There's a single, major occupant on all this land: cows.
Between pastures and cropland used to
produce feed, 41% of U.S. land in the contiguous
states revolves around livestock.
391.5 million acres = cropland
77.3 million = human food (19.7%)
52 million = idle/fallow (13.3%)
38.1 million = ethanol, biodiesel (9.7%)
127.4 million = livestock feed (32.5%)
21.5 million = wheat exports (5.5%)
62.8 million = other grain & feed
exports (16%)
13.6 million = cotton, non-food (3.5%)
Gathered together, cropland would take up more than 20% of the 48
contiguous states.
Heading into Nebraska...
Nebraska is at the lower border of
the Northern Plains, according to
the U.S. Department of
Agriculture's Natural Resources
Conservation Service, right next to
the Midwest.
58%
82%
The Northern Plains region has
15,368.4 thousand acres of
non-federal pastureland. Around
82% of this pastureland is rainfed
(not irrigated) and around 58% is
grazed by domestic livestock.
How Nebraska Farms
Nebraska's farms and ranches utilize
45.5 million acres - 93% of the state's
93%
total land area!
There are nearly 23 million acres of
rangeland and pastureland in Nebraska.
rrrr
More than one billion bushels of corn are produced here each
year, 40% of which is fed to livestock in the state. Agriculture is the
#1industryin Nebraska and cattle production represents the largest
segment of the industry. Cattle outnumber Nebraskans nearly 4 to 1
-6.64 million total cattle to 1.8 million people!
Some Quick Numbers...
Nebraska produced 11% of the Nation's corn crop in 2007
(1,426,459,812 bushels/ 12,738,519,330 total)
Nebraska produced 7% of the Nation's soybean crop in 2007
(189,547,373 bushels/2,582,423,697 total)
Nebraska produced 1% of the Nation's potato crop in 2007
(20,438 acres harvested/1,131,963 total)
Nebraska produced 4% of the Nation's wheat crop in 2007
(81,748,076 bushels/1,993,648,378 total)
Nebraska produced 6% of the Nation's beet in 2007
(1,940,000 heads/32,644,200 total)
Nebraska produced 0.5% of the Nation's milk in 2007
(1,075,000,000 1b/185,654,000,000 total)
In 2016, the National Agricultural Statistics Service
counted 48,400 farm operations in Nebraska.

Understanding the

A sustained business continuity or IT security event can result in not only financial losses
but also reputational and brand damage. Putting a price on that damage is hard to do,
and we want to help you get to those important numbers. To quantify which IT risks pose

government has led to far more infections and deaths

citizens getting restless for the reopening of their country
as the weather warms have flocked to outdoor spaces like
beaches and parks while the pub remains closed.

data.
